# On Noticing

There's a particular kind of quiet that exists only in the early morning, just before the world fully wakes up. It's not silence — there are birds, the hum of a refrigerator, the distant murmur of traffic beginning to stir — but it's a quiet that lives in the *space between things*. Most people sleep through it. I think that's a small tragedy.

We live in an age of extraordinary distraction. I don't say that as a moral judgment or a nostalgic longing for some imagined past when people were more "present." People have always been distracted — by gossip, by hunger, by the weather, by their own spiraling thoughts. But the nature of our distraction has changed. It used to be ambient, woven into the texture of daily life. Now it is engineered. Every notification, every infinite scroll, every autoplay video is designed by very smart people whose explicit job is to make you forget that you are a finite being with a limited number of mornings left.

I don't say that to depress anyone. I say it because I think the antidote is simple, and it costs nothing: *notice things*.

---

Here is something I've been thinking about lately: the texture of an orange peel. Not the inside — everyone talks about the juicy, sweet interior — but the outside. The dimpled skin. The way it resists your thumb when you first press into it, then suddenly yields, releasing a mist of oil that hits the air with an almost violent freshness. That spray contains limonene, a compound so aromatic that a single molecule landing on a receptor in your nose can trigger a cascade of memories — your grandmother's kitchen, a summer afternoon, the sticky seat of a car on a road trip you took when you were nine.

An orange peel is not important. It will not fix your career or solve your existential crisis. But I would argue that the experience of truly *noticing* it — feeling its weight in your hand, hearing the sound it makes when you tear it, watching the oil catch the light — is one of the most radically human things you can do. It is an act of rebellion against the forces that want your attention monetized and your experience flattened into content.

---

I've noticed that people often conflate *knowing about* something with *experiencing* it. We read about the Northern Lights, watch documentaries about deep ocean trenches, scroll through photographs of the Milky Way taken by telescopes that cost billions of dollars. And we feel, somehow, that we have *seen* these things. But we haven't. We've seen representations of them. We've consumed them as information. The actual experience — the cold air on your face as green light shimmers overhead, the pressure and darkness of water a mile below the surface, the vertigo of looking up and realizing that every point of light is a sun — these are entirely different categories of existence.

There's a word in Japanese — *komorebi* — that describes the sunlight filtering through leaves. It doesn't translate neatly into English because English doesn't have a single word for that specific interplay of light and shadow and foliage and breeze. But the phenomenon exists whether or not you have a word for it. It happens every day, in parks and forests and even in the strip of garden outside your apartment window. The question is whether you stop long enough to see it.

I think vocabulary shapes attention. When you learn a new word for a sensory experience, you begin to notice that experience everywhere. Before I learned the word *petrichor* — the smell of earth after rain — I knew the smell intimately but never gave it a name. Once I had the word, I started paying attention to it. I'd step outside after a storm and just *breathe*. The experience didn't change, but my relationship to it did. Language gave me a hook to hang my awareness on.

This is why I think reading poetry is not a luxury but a practical skill. Poets are professional noticers. They take the ordinary — a red wheelbarrow, a jar in Tennessee, the way light falls on a cathedral floor — and hold it up long enough for you to actually *see* it. A good poem doesn't describe something; it *restores* something. It gives you back the world you stopped seeing because you got used to it.

---

There's a concept in psychology called *hedonic adaptation*. It's the well-documented tendency for human beings to return to a baseline level of happiness regardless of positive or negative life changes. Win the lottery, and within a year you're roughly as happy as you were before. Lose a limb, and within a year you're roughly as happy as you were before. We are, in a sense, built to forget. Built to normalize. Built to stop noticing.

This is both a gift and a curse. It's a gift because it means that suffering is rarely permanent — the sharp grief that feels like it will destroy you will, with time, soften into something bearable. But it's a curse because it means that joy, too, fades into the background. The sunset you gasped at the first time you saw it from your new apartment becomes, by month three, just the thing that happens while you're making dinner.

The only antidote I've found to hedonic adaptation is *deliberate attention*. You have to choose, over and over, to see the thing as though for the first time. This is hard. It feels unnatural. Your brain is constantly whispering, *You've seen this before, move on, there might be something new and threatening over there.* But if you can resist — if you can sit with the orange peel, the light through the leaves, the sound of rain on glass — something remarkable happens. The world thickens. It becomes dense with meaning. Not because anything has changed externally, but because you have changed the quality of your attention.

---

I want to end with something I genuinely believe: the most important things in life are not the impressive things. They're not the promotions, the milestones, the achievements you put on a résumé. They're the moments of noticing — the first sip of coffee when the house is still dark, the way your dog sighs before falling asleep, the sound of someone you love laughing in another room. These moments are not scarce. They're happening all the time, constantly, in every corner of your life. The only thing scarce is your willingness to notice them.

So here is my suggestion, worth exactly what you paid for it: tomorrow morning, wake up a few minutes early. Make your coffee or your tea. Sit by a window. And just *be there*. Don't check your phone. Don't plan your day. Just notice the light. Notice the air. Notice that you are alive, and that this — right here, right now — is what being alive actually feels like.

You might be surprised by how much you've been missing.
